units.title: Signals, Channels, and Noise
units.tip: Communication systems transmit information from a source to a destination through a channel. Every channel has noise and bandwidth limits. A signal carries information; noise is unwanted interference. Understanding these basic concepts is essential for all communication systems.

exercises.question: What is a signal in communication?
exercises.answer: A physical representation of information that can be transmitted
exercises.explain: Signals carry information from a transmitter to a receiver. They can be electrical (voltage), electromagnetic (radio waves), or optical (light). The signal encodes the information.
choices: A physical representation of information that can be transmitted

exercises.question: What is noise in a communication system?
exercises.answer: Unwanted interference that distorts the signal
exercises.explain: Noise comes from thermal effects, electromagnetic interference, and other sources. It adds randomness to the signal and can cause errors if strong enough.
choices: Unwanted interference that distorts the signal

exercises.question: What is a communication channel?
exercises.answer: The medium through which a signal travels from sender to receiver
exercises.explain: Channels include copper wires, fiber optic cables, air (for radio), free space (for satellite), and other media. Every channel has limits on what signals it can carry.
choices: The medium through which a signal travels from sender to receiver

exercises.question: What is a source in communication?
exercises.answer: The device or person originating the information
exercises.explain: The source creates the information to be sent. It could be a microphone, camera, keyboard, sensor, or any device that generates data.
choices: The device or person originating the information

exercises.question: What is the destination in communication?
exercises.answer: The device or person intended to receive the information
exercises.explain: The destination receives and decodes the signal. It could be a speaker, display, printer, or any device that receives and interprets data.
choices: The device or person intended to receive the information

exercises.question: What determines how much information a channel can carry?
exercises.answer: Bandwidth and the signal-to-noise ratio
exercises.explain: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies the channel can handle. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) determines how accurately information can be recovered. Both limit channel capacity.
choices: Only the length of the cable

exercises.question: What is bandwidth?
exercises.answer: The range of frequencies a channel can transmit
exercises.explain: Bandwidth is measured in hertz. A wider bandwidth allows higher data rates. A telephone line might have a bandwidth of a few kilohertz; optical fiber can have gigahertz or more.
choices: The range of frequencies a channel can transmit

exercises.question: How is the information capacity of a channel measured?
exercises.answer: In bits per second
exercises.explain: Channel capacity tells how much data can be transmitted per second. It is measured in bits per second (bps) or kilobits per second (kbps) and depends on bandwidth and noise.

exercises.question: What is the Shannon capacity formula?
exercises.answer: Capacity equals bandwidth times the logarithm of one plus signal-to-noise ratio
exercises.explain: Shannon's formula (C = B * log2(1 + SNR)) shows that capacity increases with bandwidth and with higher SNR. It sets the theoretical maximum data rate for a channel.
choices: Capacity equals bandwidth times signal-to-noise ratio
Capacity equals signal power times bandwidth
Capacity equals bandwidth divided by noise
Capacity equals bandwidth times the logarithm of one plus signal-to-noise ratio

exercises.question: If a channel has 1000 hertz of bandwidth and an SNR of 100, what is the maximum capacity (approximately)?
exercises.answer: About 6600 bits per second
exercises.explain: Using C = B * log2(1 + SNR): C = 1000 * log2(101) = 1000 * 6.66 = 6660 bps. This shows that even with limited bandwidth, good SNR allows useful capacity.

units.title: Bandwidth and Information Rate
units.tip: Bandwidth limits the rate at which a signal can change. Higher bandwidth allows faster signal changes and therefore higher data rates. The Nyquist theorem relates bandwidth to the sampling rate needed to faithfully represent a signal.

exercises.question: Why is greater bandwidth needed for higher data rates?
exercises.answer: Higher data rates require faster signal changes, which need higher frequencies
exercises.explain: Faster signal changes contain higher frequency components. A channel must have bandwidth to handle these components or data will be lost.
choices: Higher data rates require faster signal changes, which need higher frequencies
Data rate and bandwidth are unrelated

exercises.question: What is the Nyquist theorem?
exercises.answer: A signal must be sampled at least twice per cycle to preserve all frequency information
exercises.explain: The Nyquist theorem states the minimum sampling rate is twice the highest frequency in the signal. Without this, information is lost. This is called the Nyquist rate.
choices: Sampling rate has no effect on signal recovery
Signals must be sampled at the signal frequency
A signal must be sampled at least twice per cycle to preserve all frequency information

exercises.question: A signal's highest frequency component is 4000 hertz. According to the Nyquist theorem, what is the minimum sampling rate needed to represent it?
exercises.answer: 8000 samples per second
exercises.explain: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency: 2 * 4000 = 8000 samples per second. Sampling at or above this rate captures the signal.

exercises.question: What is aliasing in digital signal processing?
exercises.answer: Distortion that occurs when sampling is slower than the Nyquist rate
exercises.explain: If you sample too slowly, high frequencies appear as lower frequencies. This cannot be undone, so it is essential to sample faster than the Nyquist rate.
choices: Distortion that occurs when sampling is slower than the Nyquist rate

exercises.question: What is the relationship between bandwidth and the number of bits per second in a digital signal?
exercises.answer: Higher bandwidth allows higher bit rates because signal changes can be faster
exercises.explain: Each bit is represented by a signal change. Faster changes need higher frequencies. Greater bandwidth means the channel can handle faster signal changes.
choices: Bit rate depends only on the modulation type
Lower bandwidth always gives higher bit rates
Higher bandwidth allows higher bit rates because signal changes can be faster

exercises.question: What is the frequency domain?
exercises.answer: A representation of a signal as a function of frequency
exercises.explain: The frequency domain shows which frequencies are present in a signal and their strengths. It is often shown as a plot of amplitude versus frequency.
choices: The power consumed by a signal
A representation of a signal as a function of frequency
The time it takes to transmit

exercises.question: What is the time domain?
exercises.answer: A representation of a signal as a function of time
exercises.explain: The time domain shows how a signal's amplitude changes over time. It is what an oscilloscope displays and what we hear when listening to audio.
choices: A representation of a signal as a function of time

exercises.question: What is the spectrum of a signal?
exercises.answer: The range of frequencies present in the signal and their amplitudes
exercises.explain: The spectrum shows all frequency components. A sine wave has one frequency; a complex signal has many. The spectrum is determined by the signal's shape.
choices: The time duration of the signal
The range of frequencies present in the signal and their amplitudes

exercises.question: What happens to the spectrum of a square wave compared to a sine wave?
exercises.answer: A square wave has many harmonic frequencies; a sine wave has one
exercises.explain: A sine wave is pure one frequency. A square wave contains the fundamental frequency plus many odd harmonics. This is why square waves need more bandwidth.
choices: A sine wave has more harmonics
A square wave has many harmonic frequencies; a sine wave has one

exercises.question: Why does a sharp-edged digital pulse train need more bandwidth than a smooth sine wave of the same repetition rate?
exercises.answer: Sharp signal transitions in digital create higher frequency components
exercises.explain: Sharp rising and falling edges contain many high frequency components. A smooth sine wave has only one frequency, so it fits in far less bandwidth.
choices: Sharp signal transitions in digital create higher frequency components

units.title: Modulation
units.tip: Modulation encodes information onto a carrier signal by varying its amplitude, frequency, or phase. Analog modulation includes AM and FM. Digital modulation uses discrete symbols: ASK varies amplitude, FSK changes frequency, PSK changes phase, and QAM combines amplitude and phase changes.

exercises.question: What is modulation?
exercises.answer: Encoding information onto a carrier signal by varying its properties
exercises.explain: Modulation takes a baseband signal (information) and encodes it onto a carrier wave. The receiver then extracts the information by demodulating.
choices: Encoding information onto a carrier signal by varying its properties

exercises.question: What is Amplitude Modulation (AM)?
exercises.answer: Varying the amplitude of a carrier wave according to the information signal
exercises.explain: In AM, the amplitude of a high-frequency carrier is modulated by the information signal. The envelope of the wave follows the original signal's shape.
choices: Varying the phase of a carrier
Varying the frequency of a carrier
Varying the amplitude of a carrier wave according to the information signal

exercises.question: What is Frequency Modulation (FM)?
exercises.answer: Varying the frequency of a carrier wave according to the information signal
exercises.explain: In FM, the frequency of the carrier changes based on the information signal. Higher amplitude information increases frequency; lower amplitude decreases it.
choices: Varying the frequency of a carrier wave according to the information signal
Varying the amplitude of a carrier
Varying the phase of a carrier

exercises.question: Why is FM less susceptible to noise than AM?
exercises.answer: Noise mainly affects amplitude; FM receivers ignore amplitude variations
exercises.explain: FM receivers extract information from frequency changes, ignoring amplitude. Noise is typically amplitude variation. AM receivers must decode amplitude, so noise directly affects the signal.
choices: Noise mainly affects amplitude; FM receivers ignore amplitude variations
FM does not use a carrier

exercises.question: Which requires more bandwidth, AM or FM?
exercises.answer: FM requires more bandwidth than AM
exercises.explain: For broadcast radio, FM typically uses many times the bandwidth of AM for the same baseband signal. This extra bandwidth provides FM's noise resistance.
choices: Bandwidth depends on the carrier frequency
FM requires more bandwidth than AM

exercises.question: What is digital modulation?
exercises.answer: Encoding digital bits onto a carrier wave using discrete symbols
exercises.explain: Digital modulation represents each bit or group of bits as a distinct signal state. Different modulation schemes use different sets of symbols.
choices: Encoding digital bits onto a carrier wave using discrete symbols

exercises.question: What is Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK)?
exercises.answer: Representing 0 and 1 by different amplitude levels of a carrier
exercises.explain: In ASK, a 0 might be no carrier signal (amplitude 0) and a 1 might be full amplitude. It is simple but susceptible to noise.
choices: Shifting the frequency of a carrier
Shifting the phase of a carrier
Representing 0 and 1 by different amplitude levels of a carrier

exercises.question: What is Frequency Shift Keying (FSK)?
exercises.answer: Representing 0 and 1 by different frequencies of a carrier
exercises.explain: In FSK, a 0 might be represented by one frequency and a 1 by another. It is more resistant to noise than ASK.
choices: Changing the phase for each symbol
Representing 0 and 1 by different frequencies of a carrier

exercises.question: What is Phase Shift Keying (PSK)?
exercises.answer: Representing bits by different phase angles of a carrier
exercises.explain: In PSK, a 0 might be 0 degrees phase and a 1 might be 180 degrees phase. More complex versions like QPSK use four phase angles for two bits per symbol.
choices: Shifting the frequency of a carrier
Shifting the amplitude of a carrier
Representing bits by different phase angles of a carrier

exercises.question: What is Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (QAM)?
exercises.answer: Combining changes in both amplitude and phase to represent more bits per symbol
exercises.explain: QAM uses a grid of amplitude and phase combinations. 16-QAM has 16 symbols, allowing 4 bits per symbol. 64-QAM has 64 symbols for 6 bits per symbol.
choices: Combining changes in both amplitude and phase to represent more bits per symbol

units.title: Multiplexing
units.tip: Multiplexing allows multiple signals to share one channel. Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM) assigns different frequency bands to each signal. Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) gives each signal a time slot. Code Division Multiplexing (CDM) assigns unique codes to each signal.

exercises.question: What is multiplexing?
exercises.answer: Sending multiple signals through a single channel
exercises.explain: Multiplexing allows efficient use of channels. Many signals share the bandwidth, frequencies, time slots, or codes, depending on the multiplexing type.
choices: Sending multiple signals through a single channel

exercises.question: What is Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM)?
exercises.answer: Assigning different frequency bands to different signals in one channel
exercises.explain: Each signal is modulated to a different carrier frequency, so all signals occupy the channel but in different frequency bands. This is used in radio broadcasting.
choices: Using the same frequency for all signals
Assigning different frequency bands to different signals in one channel

exercises.question: What is Time Division Multiplexing (TDM)?
exercises.answer: Assigning different time slots to different signals in one channel
exercises.explain: TDM rapidly switches between signals, giving each a time slot. Each signal gets the full bandwidth but only for its time slot. This is used in digital telephony.
choices: Assigning different time slots to different signals in one channel
Using different modulation for each signal

exercises.question: Why is FDM a natural fit for analog signals?
exercises.answer: Each continuous analog signal can be shifted to its own frequency band without being sampled first
exercises.explain: Analog signals are continuous, so each can be modulated onto its own carrier and sent continuously in its own band. TDM would first need to sample them.
choices: Each continuous analog signal can be shifted to its own frequency band without being sampled first

exercises.question: Why is TDM better suited for digital signals?
exercises.answer: Digital data is already discrete, so bits from several sources can be interleaved into time slots
exercises.explain: Digital data is made of discrete bits, so bits or bytes from several sources can be interleaved into time slots with no extra conversion. This is efficient and needs only one carrier.
choices: Digital data is already discrete, so bits from several sources can be interleaved into time slots

exercises.question: What is Code Division Multiplexing (CDM)?
exercises.answer: Assigning unique spreading codes to each signal so they can share the same frequency band
exercises.explain: CDM (also called CDMA) assigns each signal a unique code. The receiver uses the code to extract its signal from a mix of signals occupying the same spectrum.
choices: Assigning unique spreading codes to each signal so they can share the same frequency band

exercises.question: What is a spreading code in CDM?
exercises.answer: A pattern of bits that spreads the signal over a wider bandwidth
exercises.explain: Each user's data is multiplied by their unique spreading code, expanding it across the channel's bandwidth. The receiver multiplies by the same code to recover the original data.
choices: A pattern of bits that spreads the signal over a wider bandwidth

exercises.question: What is the main advantage of CDM?
exercises.answer: Many users can transmit at the same time in the same frequency band
exercises.explain: CDM does not need separate time slots or frequency bands for each user. Each user's unique code lets the receiver extract that user's signal even while others transmit.
choices: Many users can transmit at the same time in the same frequency band

exercises.question: What happens if two users' spreading codes are identical in CDM?
exercises.answer: The receiver cannot distinguish between them and gets both signals mixed together
exercises.explain: Spreading codes must be orthogonal (uncorrelated) to enable separation. If codes are identical, the receiver sees both users' signals as one.
choices: The receiver cannot distinguish between them and gets both signals mixed together

exercises.question: How many users can share a CDM channel?
exercises.answer: As many as there are unique orthogonal spreading codes available
exercises.explain: The number of users is limited by the number of distinct orthogonal codes. More codes allow more simultaneous users. The spreading factor and code length determine code availability.
choices: As many as there are unique orthogonal spreading codes available

units.title: Noise and Error Management
units.tip: Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) measures signal strength relative to noise. Higher SNR allows more reliable communication. Error detection finds corrupted data using parity bits and checksums. Error correction uses redundancy to fix errors without retransmission.

exercises.question: What is signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)?
exercises.answer: The ratio of signal power to noise power
exercises.explain: SNR is measured in decibels (dB). SNR = 10 * log10(Signal Power / Noise Power). Higher SNR means a stronger signal relative to noise, enabling more reliable transmission.
choices: The ratio of signal power to noise power

exercises.question: How does SNR affect the bit error rate?
exercises.answer: Higher SNR results in lower bit error rate
exercises.explain: With higher SNR, the signal is clearer relative to noise, reducing the chance of bit errors. Better SNR allows detection of weaker signals and use of more efficient modulation.
choices: Higher SNR results in lower bit error rate
Lower SNR gives lower error rate
SNR has no effect on error rate

exercises.question: What sources contribute to noise in a communication channel?
exercises.answer: Thermal noise, electromagnetic interference, and other environmental sources
exercises.explain: Thermal noise comes from random electron motion in conductors. EMI comes from nearby electrical equipment. Cosmic radiation and other sources also contribute.
choices: Thermal noise, electromagnetic interference, and other environmental sources

exercises.question: Why is SNR expressed in decibels?
exercises.answer: Because power ratios are very large and decibels compress the scale logarithmically
exercises.explain: Decibels (dB) allow easy comparison of ratios. A signal might be 10,000 times the noise power, which equals 40 dB. This logarithmic scale is convenient for communication engineering.
choices: Because power ratios are very large and decibels compress the scale logarithmically

exercises.question: If a signal has 1000 watts of power and noise has 10 watts, what is the SNR in decibels?
exercises.answer: 20 decibels
exercises.explain: SNR = 10 * log10(1000/10) = 10 * log10(100) = 10 * 2 = 20 dB. This shows a good signal-to-noise ratio.

exercises.question: What is error detection?
exercises.answer: Adding extra bits to a message to identify if corruption occurred
exercises.explain: Error detection uses redundancy to detect errors but not fix them. If an error is detected, the data is discarded or retransmitted.
choices: Adding extra bits to a message to identify if corruption occurred

exercises.question: What is a parity bit?
exercises.answer: An extra bit added to make the total number of ones even or odd
exercises.explain: Parity bits detect single-bit errors. Even parity means the total number of ones is even; odd parity means it is odd. If parity changes, an error occurred.
choices: A bit that indicates the frequency
An extra bit added to make the total number of ones even or odd

exercises.question: What is a checksum?
exercises.answer: A value computed from data to verify its integrity
exercises.explain: A checksum is computed by adding or using other operations on data bits. If the message is corrupted, the checksum will not match, indicating an error.
choices: A value computed from data to verify its integrity

exercises.question: What is error correction?
exercises.answer: Adding extra bits so errors can be identified and fixed without retransmission
exercises.explain: Error correction uses more redundancy than detection. The extra bits allow the receiver to identify which bits are wrong and correct them.
choices: Adding extra bits so errors can be identified and fixed without retransmission

exercises.question: Why is error correction important for wireless and satellite communication?
exercises.answer: Retransmission is slow or impractical due to long delays and poor connectivity
exercises.explain: In wireless and satellite systems, retransmission is expensive due to long propagation delays or poor links. Error correction allows reliable transmission without asking for retransmission.
choices: Retransmission is slow or impractical due to long delays and poor connectivity

units.title: Antennas and Transmission
units.tip: Antennas convert electrical signals into electromagnetic waves for transmission, or receive electromagnetic waves and convert them back to electrical signals. The size and shape of an antenna relate to the wavelength of the signal. Understanding antenna fundamentals helps explain how radio, television, and wireless systems work.

exercises.question: What is an antenna?
exercises.answer: A device that converts electrical signals to electromagnetic waves or vice versa
exercises.explain: An antenna is the interface between a transmission line and free space. A transmitting antenna radiates EM waves; a receiving antenna captures them.
choices: A device that converts electrical signals to electromagnetic waves or vice versa

exercises.question: How is antenna length related to wavelength?
exercises.answer: Common antenna lengths are half-wavelength or quarter-wavelength
exercises.explain: A half-wave dipole antenna is about half a wavelength long. A quarter-wave antenna is about one-quarter wavelength. These lengths resonate with the radio frequency.
choices: Common antenna lengths are half-wavelength or quarter-wavelength
Antennas are always one full wavelength
Length depends only on the power
Antenna length does not depend on wavelength

exercises.question: What is the relationship between frequency and wavelength?
exercises.answer: Wavelength equals the speed of light divided by frequency
exercises.explain: The formula is wavelength = c / f, where c is the speed of light (about 300,000 km/s). Higher frequencies have shorter wavelengths.
choices: Wavelength equals the speed of light divided by frequency

exercises.question: For a frequency of 1000 megahertz, what is the wavelength?
exercises.answer: 0.3 meters (30 centimeters)
exercises.explain: Using wavelength = c / f: wavelength = 300,000,000 m/s / 1,000,000,000 Hz = 0.3 meters. This shows why UHF antennas are relatively small.

exercises.question: Why must an antenna size match the wavelength of the signal?
exercises.answer: Antennas work efficiently when their length resonates with the wavelength
exercises.explain: Resonance occurs when antenna dimensions are a fraction of wavelength. A half-wave antenna at the right frequency radiates efficiently. Mismatched sizes lead to poor radiation.
choices: Frequency does not affect antenna design
Antennas work efficiently when their length resonates with the wavelength

exercises.question: What is the path loss in radio propagation?
exercises.answer: The reduction in signal power as it travels through space
exercises.explain: Path loss occurs because the transmitter's power spreads over an increasingly large area as distance increases. Path loss is proportional to the square of the distance and frequency.
choices: The reduction in signal power as it travels through space
Loss from using a short antenna

exercises.question: How does signal strength decrease with distance in free space?
exercises.answer: Inversely with the square of the distance
exercises.explain: Signal power decreases as 1/d^2. If you double the distance, the signal is one-fourth as strong. This is the inverse square law of wave propagation.
choices: Inversely with the square of the distance

exercises.question: What is fading in wireless communication?
exercises.answer: Temporary reduction in received signal strength due to reflections and obstacles
exercises.explain: Fading occurs when signals bounce off buildings and terrain, arriving at the receiver from multiple paths with different delays. These paths can reinforce or cancel each other.
choices: Temporary reduction in received signal strength due to reflections and obstacles
Increase in transmitter power over time
Loss of signal due to distance

exercises.question: What is multipath propagation?
exercises.answer: When a signal reaches the receiver via multiple reflected paths with different delays
exercises.explain: Multipath occurs when reflections from buildings and terrain reach the receiver along with, or instead of, the direct signal, each with a different delay. This can cause interference and fading.
choices: When a signal reaches the receiver via multiple reflected paths with different delays

exercises.question: Why is higher frequency more susceptible to path loss than lower frequency?
exercises.answer: A receiving antenna of fixed design captures less of the spread-out power at higher frequencies
exercises.explain: Free-space spreading depends only on distance. The frequency term in path loss appears because an antenna's effective area shrinks with wavelength, so it captures less power at higher frequencies. Higher frequencies are also absorbed and blocked more by obstacles and atmosphere.
choices: Frequency does not affect path loss
Lower frequency antennas are always better
A receiving antenna of fixed design captures less of the spread-out power at higher frequencies
Higher frequency waves travel more slowly
